hooks.text: In 1957, astronomers logged a tiny faint star that wasn't a star.
Entry 618 looked like a tiny faint blue star in 1957.
A faint blue star catalogued in 1957 was actually a cosmic monster.

title: The Faint Blue Star That Was 40 Billion Suns
description: In 1957, entry TON 618 was catalogued as an ordinary faint blue star. Decades later, astronomers discovered an ultramassive black hole shining with the light of 140 trillion Suns.

beats.text: In 1957, astronomers logged a tiny faint star that wasn't a star.
beats.visual: photographic survey plate showing faint stellar point sources, 1957

beats.text: Braulio Iriarte and Enrique Chavira recorded entry 618 at Mexico's Tonantzintla Observatory as a white dwarf.
beats.visual: photograph of the Tonantzintla Observatory Schmidt telescope, Mexico, 1957

beats.text: In 1970, radio signals from Bologna and spectra from McDonald Observatory revealed entry 618 was a quasar.
beats.visual: photograph of the Northern Cross Radio Telescope array near Bologna, 1970

beats.text: Its central beacon shines with the brilliance of 140 trillion Suns, drowning out its host galaxy entirely.
beats.visual: artist's concept of an extremely luminous active galactic nucleus and quasar accretion disk

beats.text: Infalling gas whirls around the core at speeds up to 10,500 kilometers per second, lighting up a nebula three times wider than the Milky Way.
beats.visual: illustration of an immense Lyman-alpha nebula surrounding a supermassive black hole

beats.text: Depending on the spectral line analyzed, astronomers estimate its central black hole contains between 40.7 and 66 billion solar masses.
beats.visual: diagram comparing the event horizon size of TON 618 to the Solar System

beats.text: Light from this ultramassive engine traveled 10.8 billion years to reach Earth, where entry 618 looked like a tiny faint star.
beats.visual: deep space field photograph of distant quasars across cosmic time

better_than_last: Applied exact mass range attribution (40.7 to 66 billion Suns) directly in beat 6 to handle disputed spectroscopic measurements accurately while preserving maximum scale impact.
